core_principles.text: Using an unstable implement utilizing water inertia during a bicep curl increases instability in the paraspinal and deltoid muscles for both men and women.
Men experience greater overall instability in the biceps compared to women when performing curls with an unstable water-filled implement.

specific_findings.text: Paraspinal muscle instability during the bicep curl was significantly higher in the 50% open water condition (CV = 26.5  14.5) and 100% open water condition (CV = 27.1  9.9) compared to the stable condition (CV = 15.0  9.1).
Deltoid muscle instability was greatest at the 100% open water setting (CV = 38.5  23.2) compared to the stable setting (CV = 21.0  7.5).
For the bicep, men showed greater overall instability (CV = 30.9  17.0) compared to women (CV = 22.9  8.4) when using the unstable water-filled implement.

Percent MVC activated in the bicep was significantly greater for women (50% open = 97.7  57.6, 100% open = 88.1  55.6, stable = 87.0  50.1) compared to men (50% open = 39.5  17.0, 100% open = 38.3  18.3, stable = 31.8  11.1).

Percent MVC activated in the paraspinal muscles was significantly greater for women (50% open = 36.7  22.3, 100% open = 47.5  29.0, stable = 38.6  23.9) compared to men (50% open = 15.1  10.0, 100% open = 16.2  8.8, stable = 14.3  9.6).
